name: Citrulline malate
lead: Citrulline malate (CM) is a supplement that combines the amino acid L-citrulline with malic acid. Citrulline is a non-essential alpha-amino acid and a key intermediate in the urea cycle, the pathway mammals use to convert ammonia to urea; it is also a byproduct of nitric oxide production from arginine [1]. Its name comes from citrullus, the Latin word for watermelon, from which it was first isolated in 1914 [1].

CM is a common ingredient in pre-workout powders, where it is promoted for muscle 'pump', blood flow, endurance in resistance sets and recovery [2][14]. The proposed mechanism is increased nitric oxide and blood flow to active muscle, with possible effects on ammonia handling and on ATP production through malate [2].

Published evidence on exercise performance is described by reviewers as equivocal [2]. Wikipedia states that there is no good evidence that taking citrulline is effective or safe for athletic performance and that it has no confirmed clinical uses [1]. No study in the sources reviewed here has shown that CM increases muscle size.
infobox: Amino acid / organic acid salt (L-citrulline + malic acid)
Dietary supplement; not an approved prescription drug [1]

paras: Citrulline malate is used by lifters and other athletes before training for pump, blood flow and fatigue resistance. T Nation's own pre-workouts list CM among their ingredients, for example a formula containing 6 g of citrulline malate [12][13], and the site describes the compound as reducing lactic acid and ammonia buildup, increasing nitric oxide production and aiding ATP regeneration [14].

Forum members also discuss citrulline alongside erectile dysfunction medication and blood pressure, with some reporting adding citrulline to daily tadalafil or finding it helped their blood pressure [15][16]. Citrulline is also sold as a topical moisturising agent and hair-styling ingredient [1].

A critical review of citrulline malate and exercise performance noted that a single acute 8 g dose has been the most common approach and has produced equivocal results, and attributed the disparity to differing testing protocols, dosing strategy and recently identified quality-control problems with some manufacturers' stated citrulline-to-malate ratios [2].

A systematic review and meta-analysis of foods containing nitrate, polyphenols, arginine or citrulline in endurance performance found no effect for citrulline-rich foods (three studies), while nitrate- and polyphenol-rich foods showed trivial benefits [3]. A systematic review and three-level meta-analysis of citrulline malate and exercise performance has also been published [4]. A 2023 study examined acute L-citrulline on resistance exercise performance and muscle oxygenation in recreationally trained men and women [5].

Wikipedia says there is no good evidence on safety for performance use [1]. Citrulline raises arginine and nitric oxide availability, which is why forum users who take blood pressure or erectile dysfunction drugs ask about interactions [15][16]. A registered trial is testing L-citrulline with tadalafil in mild to moderate erectile dysfunction (NCT07642505) [17]. Disorders of citrulline metabolism, such as adult-onset citrullinemia and the HHH syndrome, are described in the medical literature but concern genetic urea-cycle conditions rather than supplement use [6][7].

Citrulline is converted to arginine, a substrate for nitric oxide synthase; citrulline is released when nitric oxide is made [1]. The performance hypothesis rests on nitric oxide-driven blood flow, improved ammonia homeostasis and malate's possible role in ATP production, none of which the review considered established for performance [2].
The foundation literature on nitric oxide synthesis from L-arginine in vascular endothelium dates to 1988 [8].

The formula of citrulline is H2NC(O)NH(CH2)3CH(NH2)CO2H [1]. Gastroenterologists described the substance in the late nineteenth century; Japanese researchers Yataro Koga and Ryo Otake isolated it from watermelon in 1914 and it was further characterised in 1930 [1]. Citrullination of proteins is a separate post-translational modification [1].

Exercise: the critical review, the endurance-food meta-analysis and the three-level meta-analysis above [2][3][4], plus a single-blind crossover trial of a multi-ingredient pre-workout (containing citrulline malate, beta-alanine, arginine alpha-ketoglutarate, taurine, tyrosine and caffeine) against caffeine alone on bench press [9]. A registered trial compared L-citrulline and citrulline malate on neuromuscular performance in resistance-trained adults (NCT05183893) [18].

Other populations: trials of L-citrulline in asthma (NCT01715844, NCT02943161), pulmonary hypertension in premature infants (NCT03542812), MELAS (NCT03952234), sickle cell vaso-occlusive pain (NCT06635902), COPD with malnutrition (NCT06212765), preeclampsia in pregnancy, and cold exposure and hypertension (NCT02104375, NCT01462591) are registered or published [10][19][20][21][22][23][24][25][26].

timeline.event: Citrulline is first isolated from watermelon by Yataro Koga and Ryo Otake [1].
Nitric oxide is shown to be synthesised from L-arginine by vascular endothelium [8].
A critical review describes equivocal evidence for citrulline malate and exercise performance [2].

lore.intro: On T Nation citrulline malate appears chiefly as a pre-workout ingredient and in threads about blood pressure and erectile function [12][14][15].

claims.claim: Citrulline malate boosts nitric oxide, pump and blood flow
claims.believers: Forum and product copy describe citrulline malate as increasing nitric oxide production and reducing lactic acid and ammonia buildup [14].
claims.experts: A critical review calls the performance evidence equivocal and notes that nitric oxide-related mechanisms are not firmly established for performance [2].

claims.claim: It improves endurance and reps in the gym
claims.believers: Users add it to pre-workouts to support volume; one reports taking it daily for months and attributing improved fatigue symptoms to citrulline [27].
claims.experts: A meta-analysis found no effect for citrulline-rich foods on endurance [3]; the CM review describes inconsistent trials and dose-ratio quality issues [2].

claims.claim: Citrulline helps blood pressure and erectile function alongside tadalafil
claims.believers: Posters report adding citrulline to daily Cialis or note lower blood pressure with citrulline [15][16].
claims.experts: A trial of L-citrulline with tadalafil in erectile dysfunction is registered [17]; no completed result is in the sources cited here.

claims.claim: Citrulline is gentler on mood than arginine
claims.believers: One poster said they believed citrulline lacks arginine's reported mood effects but could not recall the source [28].
claims.experts: No published study cited here compares their effects on mood.
